To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
self-organized frameworks can be used to create multifunctional e-fibers with high sensitivity, selectivity, and reliability for sensing and filtration applications.
the self-organized frameworks (SOFTs) on textiles can be used for the detection of toxic gases at ppm levels, and for the capture and filtration of these gases.

we have developed an innovative and simple method for integrating conductive 2D MOFs into fabrics, which can be used to detect and differentiate important gases at ppm levels and to filter and capture these gases.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing a new class of e-textiles with multifunctionality for wearable electronics.
developing a simple and rapid method for fabricating multifuctional e-textiles with the capacity to sense and capture gases.
the development of a new generation of e-textiles that are capable of sensing and capturing analytes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

this is a new approach to the fabrication of multifunctional e-fabrics with a wide range of potential applications in the areas of wearable electronics, environmental monitoring, and personal protective equipment.
we have demonstrated a new strategy for the fabrication of multifunctional e- textiles that integrate sensing, capture, and filtration of gases.

the SOFT approach provides a general and scalable platform for the fabrication of multifunctional e- textiles with the ability to sense, capture, and filter analytes, which can be used in the design of next-generation wearable devices.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the integration of MOFs on fabrics through direct solution-based self-assembly represents an effective approach for developing multifunctional e-wearable devices with the capacity to sense, capture, and filter gases.
we have demonstrated the first example of a multifunctional e- textile for simultaneous detection, filtration, and uptake of gases.

we developed a simple and rapid method of making e-textiles that can sense, capture, and filter analytes, and we demonstrated that this method can be used to make e-textiles that are capable of detecting and filtering important gaseous pollutants at the ppb level.
The main takeaway from our work is that

simple solution-phase assembly can be used for the rapid integration of functional materials onto fabrics, enabling the development of multifunctional e- textiles with the potential to be used as wearable sensors for environmental monitoring and personal health.
self-assembly is an efficient approach to integrate multifunctionality into textiles, enabling the development of wearable devices for sensing, filtration, and capture of analytes.
the SOFT-approach provides an efficient strategy for the fabrication of multifunctional, wearable electronic devices that are capable of sensing, capturing, and filtering analytes.
